The loin and lean meat of pork are chopped together, and then ground in a metate, removing the sinews and tendons as they appear: the ground mixture is then kneaded with clove powder, cinnamon, and cumin, a little saffron ground with garlic and chopped peppermint: everything is mixed well with a little butter and one raw egg, and it was chopped with the meat, and more butter.
Once they are cooked, and just before being taken to the table, the broth is thickened with flour and egg yolks, according to the quantity.
ROYAL MEATBALLS.

Everything incorporated, the meatballs are formed, and ham and hard-boiled egg are placed in the middle. For the broth, garlic, chopped poblano chiles or tornachiles shredded, slices of onion, and roasted and ground xitoraate will be fried in butter: once the frying has browned a little, it is seasoned with salt and water, capers, and spices of the same kind that were mixed with the meat, vinegar, and oil in small quantity are added.

DRIED PORK MEATBALLS. Prepared in any of the indicated ways, mainly those cooked in a tomato broth, they are left to consume it at two fires, and are served hot, garnished with chili peppers and olives.
CHICKEN MEATBALLS. Raw chicken breasts are chopped, seasoned with salt, and mixed with onion and very finely chopped tomatoes, making the meatballs, which are fried in butter. For the broth, toasted and ground almonds, and also toasted and ground bread, are fried, adding chicken broth: the meatballs are put in it to finish cooking, without letting the broth thicken too much.
CHICKEN AND EGG YOLK MEATBALLS. The breasts are prepared and seasoned as in the previous article, mixed with chopped garlic and parsley, saffron, cloves, pepper, cinnamon, and ground cumin and cooked and crumbled egg yolks: adding a little oil and vinegar, the meatballs are formed, which will have inside raisins, ham, or hard-boiled egg, and are fried in butter. They are taken out to make the broth, putting in the same butter, chopped onion, roasted and ground tomatoes with raisins, spices from those put in the meat, capers, and chicken broth with a little oil. When this broth is boiling, the meatballs are added to finish cooking, without letting the broth reduce too much.
These same are varied, made with almond sauce or raisin and golden bread sauce, or liver sauce. [See these articles in their place].

a pot. When taking it to the table oil, chopped very finely parsley, chilitos, olives

amounts of walnuts and almonds are ground, with

and raw garlic; as soon as everything is
very finely ground, it is fried in oil with

the time of serving, putting on top
chopped parsley, chiles, olives
and other garnishes.

giving it a boil with sugar and lemon,
it is ready to be served with any roast, especially of fowl.

COD IN TOMATO JUICE. It
is soaked from the previous day changing
waters, and the next day it is put in
lukewarm water until the time to cook,
then crumbled and removing the bones and backbone: it is put to
cook in oil with tomato juice,
onions and garlic chopped very finely,
and chili also chopped, but very desvenado.
COD WITH BREAD CRUMBS AND CHEESE.
They are fried very well in oil onion and
parsley chopped finely, sour and ground tomatoes, adding a little
of bread crumbs, pepper, oregano and
cheese also grated. In this sauce
the fish is put to cook in large portions with oil, chilitos and olives.
COD ON BREAD SLICES*.
In the amount of oil proportionate to the fish that one wants to cook,
some garlic are fried until they burn, and
then they are removed: enough chopped onion and some green chilies whole are put in the oil: when the onion is acitrone, roasted tomatoes are put,
peeled and mar chopped, in proportion of eight large and ripe tomatoes for each fish, the corresponding salt, pieces of ancho chili toasted in butter and bread slices
likewise, with a little of bread soaked in vinegar and ground. Everything being very fried, the cooked and deboned cod is put there, leaving it
boil a little, and to serve it is arranged in a platter on slices of
cold bread without browning, with the broth or sauce on top.

CATFISH IN TOMATO SAUCE.
After the catfish is well cleaned with ash, so that it becomes white, the spine is removed and the bones from the center of the head are taken out; it is dried well with a cloth, so that it remains dry, it is rolled in flour, it is placed in a pan that has sufficient capacity, butter is added and over a low fire that does not burn the butter too much, it is put to fry and left until it is well browned on the bottom side: then it is carefully turned so that it does not fall apart, and when it is browned on both sides, some ripe tomatoes are roasted, a little pepper and some garlic are ground, the tomatoes are peeled very well, the ground pepper and garlic and hot butter (which is not the one in which the catfish was fried) are poured over them. Once they have been fried well with that butter, a little water is added, leaving it to boil until the tomato dissolves well, and when it is seasoned, it is poured over the catfish, and on top raw cooking oil is added, and it is left to rest in the heat until the time to serve it.

BOTARGA. A type of sausage made from the eggs of the sargo, as the cabial is made from those of the sturgeon. (See SARGO ROE.
BRASA (to boil or roast on the). An excellent method of cooking meats that are thus of a notable taste, because they lose none of their juices, since in this way no sensible evaporation results.
The piece to be cooked is covered with slices of fat or ham, or of meat; a small assorted bunch, parsnips or tomatoes, onions and spices are added, with a glass of white wine and another of broth, according to the size of the piece to be cooked and basted, many fires being necessary for the cooking to be completed;
BUD -88- BUD
since it must be verified gradually over two gentle fires.
BRETON. A variety of cabbage, which is eaten only in salad. (See salad of bretons), but here bretons generally refers to the stalks of common cabbage, when allowed to flower, and they are also eaten in salad.
BROCCOLI. Italian cabbage, a variety of common cabbage. With it the same stews are prepared as with cabbage (see CABBAGE); but here it is used only in salad. (See salad of broccoli.)
BUCHES of Pastiano. Equal parts of mutton and pork meat are chopped as for meatballs, and raisins, sesame, pepper, chopped apples, cloves, pine nuts, cinnamon, saffron and garlic are added to the mince; everything is beaten very well and kneaded with butter. Small paper cases the size of cigar papers are made, filled and put to cook over two fires: while they cook, some very red tomatoes are roasted and chopped with garlic, parsley and mint, to make the broth with this and spices of the same kind that were added to the meat, and the buches are placed in it.
PUDDING. It is a preparation entirely different from those made with blood or pork meat and other ingredients, known by the names of blood sausage or morcón, chorizos, longaniza, etc., although in both cases the intestines are filled with the blood and minced meat.

JVf ARO. Species of sea crab, see CANGREJO.)
CAMARON. Some confuse it with the crab, the lobster and the small sea shrimp; but the one legitimately called shrimp is a crustacean of the size and thickness of the little finger, although there are also smaller ones, which are of less value in commerce, despite being equal in flavor.
Fry it in oil: take it out and place it on the plate, then pour over it fried garlic, finely chopped parsley, and oil and vinegar, seasoned with salt.
SHRIMP MARINIERE STYLE.
Clean the shrimp raw, and put them to fry in butter until they begin to brown. Roast some ripe tomatoes, and after peeling them, grind them very well; fry them with the shrimp; add a little good vinegar or red wine, and a piece of sugar: let it boil until the broth reduces, and serve cold, drained of the butter, or hot.

Small, white, and stringless ones are selected: once cooked, they are split lengthwise, and between the two halves, minced pork meat is placed (see PICADILLO for filling). They are dipped in beaten egg, and fried in lard: they are served dry, or in xitomate broth, like that of the stuffed chiles, or in nogada. (See) poblan camotes. After being cooked, peeled, mashed, and sprinkled with water, the camotes are passed through a sieve; and with an equal amount of their weight in sugar, a clarified syrup is made to the setting point in water: then the camote is mixed in, stirring well until it dissolves: everything is returned to the heat until it reaches the point of releasing from the pot, adding a little orange blossom water. Once the paste is cool, the small camotes are shaped, sprinkling sifted sugar on the hand so that they do not stick. others.

mutton (Meatballs of). Two parts of mutton pulp, one of pork loin, and one of head are taken, and both are finely chopped. After chopping, a small piece of bread soaked in vinegar is added, and everything together is ground very well, removing all the sinews and skins that resist. Then, some garlic cloves are fried, and a piece of bread is toasted; some ripe tomatoes are roasted, and all this is ground in a little vinegar, and fried in the fat in which the garlic was browned. When all this is well fried, cloves, pepper, cinnamon, and cumin are ground; the roasted mutton is added, and it is turned in the frying, adding a suitable amount of cooking oil, a little meat broth or water is added, along with some cooked and chopped onions, olives, tornachiles, and a little oregano, and it is left to season until it thickens sufficiently.

Clarificado el almíbar, hecho con una

bre: cuando se haya enfriado, se le
añaden ocho yemas batidas como para
huevos reales: se vuelve á la lumbre
para que se cueza el huevo, y se vacia
en un platón, dorándose como se dijo
en los artículos anteriores.

FRIED QUAIL WITH TOMATO SAUCE. The quails being prepared, they are fried in butter with slices of salchichón and sausages, slices of ham, and the corresponding salt: when ready, roasted and ground tomatoes, chopped parsley, more parsley, cloves, cinnamon, and pepper, ground, and water and white wine in equal quantities are added: when the quails are well cooked and the sauce thickened, they are served with tender leaves of rosemary on top, chilies, and olives.

QUAIL EN PAPER ON THE GRILL. Cooked in water with salt, they are drained and stuffed with ham, brushed with oil, and covered with breadcrumbs mixed with salt and ground pepper: they are wrapped in well-oiled paper and placed on the grill over very gentle heat, so that the paper does not burn, and as soon as they are browned, they are removed and served.

vaca, ternera, carnero, cerdo, &c, sazonadas con especias y yerbas picadas,
y guisadas de distintos modos. Estos
guisos se llaman también chuletas.

chuletas ije ternera ) (Véanse en

xero. muele la carne con toda cía
se de especias y se hacen unas larguitas que se ponen á cocer en una sartén con agua y sal, dejándose sancochar consumida el agua: se frien des
pites con huevo cortado y bc echan
por último en un caldillo hecho con
harina frita, vino blanco, vinagie, un
poquito de azúcar y otro de pimienta.

CHULETAS ADOBADAS Y EMPANADAS.
Se hacen unas rebanadas medianas de
pulpa de carnero y se dejan de un dia
para otro en un adobo hecho con una
taza de zumo de naranja, otra de aceite y dos de vinagre con pimienta y sal
molidas; al dia siguiente se sacan del
adobo y se cuecen á la parrilla; se revuelcan después en pan rallado con
sal molida y pimienta, y se vuelven á
la parrilla para que se asen. Se sirven
en salsa de cebolla con aceite, vinagre
y orégano.

Se hacen lo mismo de carne de vaca.

sin adobar. Se deja manir el trozo
de carnero de donde se han de sacar
las chuletas, se le quita el hueso, el
pellejo, los tendones y la gordura; se
cortan las tajadas, se aplanan con. un
machete mojado, y se redondean con
el cuchillo; se mojan después en aceite ó en manteca derretida, se empanan y se cuecen á la parrilla.
CHULETAS DE CARNERO PICADAS Y
heladas. Se cortan trozos grandes y
después de mechados con jamón, se
pasan por manteca para que se afir-
men; se dejan escurrir y se preparan
nuevamente con manteca al fuego; se
dejan enfriar, se recortan y redondean,
y se vuelven á la cazuela con un trozo de gelatina y un poco de caldo, envolviéndolas en papel enmantecado:
cuando estén de buen color y bien heladas, se aderezan con coscorrones fritos y se sirven con cualquiera salsa.

xitomate. Se asan á la parrilla y se
aderezan en un platón, en forma de
corona, interpolándose con tostadas
fritas, y añadiéndose la salsa de xito-
mate llamada de ángeles.

EMPINADO. Although this broth can be applied to various meats, it is common to prepare it for chicken or pork, and for this purpose roasted tomatoes, cooked tomatoes, very few also cooked green chiles, roasted garlic, and pineapple are ground: all the ground mixture is fried, adding small pieces of ham and chopped pineapple, and the cooked pork loin with the water in which it was cooked is placed there: it is seasoned with sufficient salt and
ENC
when it has given some boils, cooked corn kernels, raisins, almonds, pine nuts, and a small piece of sugar are added, thickening the broth with ground pitaya. When serving, it is garnished with small chiles and olives.
It is also made by placing the pork loin raw with a little water so that it cooks in this broth, which gives it an exquisite taste.
EMPINADO FOR CHICKENS OR OTHER BIRDS.
Pineapple, tomatoes, golden garlic, toasted bread in butter, cinnamon, and cloves are ground; everything is put to fry, and then the necessary water is added to make the broth, in which, already seasoned with salt, the quarters of chicken or young chickens are put to cook.
empinado with vinegar. A pineapple, after peeled, is divided into two halves; one is put to cook, and the other is ground with roasted tomatoes, and the ground mixture is put to fry with chopped garlic, cloves, cinnamon, pepper, cilantro, and saffron, all ground: then the cooked pineapple is added in pieces, a little vinegar and sugar, and the water in which the birds, which are to be stewed in this broth, have been cooked: these are cut into quarters, seasoned with salt, and thickened with toasted bread.
ENCARBONADOS of milk. A handful of well-ground nixtamal is poured into four quarts of milk and, sweetened, it is strained through a sieve: it is then put to cook with a little chopped nut or almond and some strips of cinnamon, giving it a higher consistency than that of blancmange.

COLESLAW WITH ONIONS.
After the cabbages have been well cleaned of
all green or tough leaves, they are put to cook with onions cut into
quarters, water, and white salt. They are fried
in a casserole with oil and butter
in equal amounts, tomato, xil omate,
garlic, and parsley, all chopped, and spices of all kinds, ground, except saffron.
When everything is well fried, the cabbages and onions that were cooked are added there to be fried as well, and when done, they are served hot with oil
and vinegar, seasoned with salt and powdered oregano.

CAULIFLOWER SALAD IN PIECES.
The cauliflower is boiled with white salt
and crushed garlic cloves; then
they are fried in a pan with some sliced garlic cloves in oil, these are removed when they have browned, and
the cauliflower, divided into its florets, is fried there. Once it is browned, it is sprinkled with pepper, salt and oregano, and
garnished with chillies, olives and chopped
onion.
CAULIFLOWER SALAD WITH TOMATO SAUCE. After the cauliflower has been well cooked,
it is divided into its stalks, slicing lengthwise those that are
very large; they are placed on the platter and
covered with a sauce made as follows. Roasted tomatoes are ground,
dissolved in vinegar, enough salt is added and oregano is sprinkled; some cooked onions are coarsely chopped, and a sufficient amount of oil is stirred in; the cauliflower is covered with this sauce and garnished with slices of peeled avocado, quarters of cooked onion, chopped tornachiles, quarters of small zucchini and olives.

mixed salad. Peel bergamot pears, quinces, and pear-shaped fruits, core them, dice them into small cubes, and put them to cook in water with a little sugar and some slices of cinnamon. Half-cooked, remove them from the fire and drain; add to them pitted and chopped raisins, cleaned and toasted almonds, and pine nuts, and sprinkle with cinnamon powder, moistening with vinegar sweetened with sugar, or with muscat wine.

SALAD OF XITOMATE, WHICH THEY CALL aguacabiole. Cook ripe xitomates and green chiles, peel both, and grind them; dissolve in good vinegar, add chopped chiles in vinegar and mashed cooked onions: chop avocado into small pieces, add the appropriate amount of salt and sufficient oil; place in the dish and garnish on top with tornachiles in vinegar divided into quarters, olives, plenty of slices of peeled avocado, and powdered oregano.

ESCABECHE FRIO Ó* CALIENTE PARA
el mismo día. Después de limpio
el pescado y cortado en raciones, se
revolcará en harina y se freirá con hue-
vo. Después se tomará un tanto de
vinagre y otro de agua, y se sazonará
con azúcar. Se molerán azafráu, pi-
mienta, ajengibre tostado y una poca
de sal fina y se deshará todo en el vi-
nagre aguado, procurándose que no sea
mucho el caldillo. Se echará allí el
pescado y se pondrá al fuego para que
dé un hervor, agregándole tornachiles
cortados en cuarterones. Se apartará
del fuego y se le echará bastante vi-
nagre, con ruedas de lima cocidas, y
unos chiles verdes desvenados. Se
sirve frió ó caliente, y es para el mis-
mo dia.
ESCABECHE PARA BESUGO . Después
de cortada la cabeza del besugo y
escamado, se troza en raciones y se
fríe en aceite con unos cuantos ajos:
cuando ya esté dorado, se apartará y
se dejará enfriar. Se tomará el jugo
de doce naranjas agrias y se le agrega-
rá un cuartillo de vinagre y dos de a-
gua; se molerán clavo, azafrán, pimien-
ta y sal, se formará con esto el caldi-
diilo y se pondiá al fuego procurando
que no hierva. Cuando esté sazona-
do se apea, y en enfriándose se echan
los trozos de besugo, guardándolos
bien tapados. Se sirve frió ó caliente
sin agregarle otra cosa que ajos asa-
dos en manteca.
ESCABECHE PARA PE8CADO APREN-
SADO. Se corta el pescado fresco, sea
de la clase que fuere, en tajadas de
un tamaño regular, y se pone á desfle-
mar con naranja agria ó con limón:
un poco antea de que se fria, se echa
en agua para que se limpie y remoje.
Se pone con aceite una cazuela a la
lumbre, y estando bien caliente, se
echan en ella ajos con su cascara, ma-
chacados, en suficiente cantidad para
ponerse en camas entre las tajadas
del pescado en el cuñete: cuando se
hayan frito se apartan, y en el mismo
aceite se fríe el pescado sin que se do-
re ni se tueste, para que no se endu-

espinacas en seco. Bien cocidas
las espinacas con sal de la tierra, se sa-
can y se lavan en agua fria: después se
exprimen en un lienzo, se pone una ca-

Two terms by which
the various qualities
or classes of cheese are distinguished (see CHEESE), it being sufficient to note here, that by fresh is understood
the cheese little pressed, with
salt or without it, which is made to be eaten immediately, as it does not keep long, and is usually of small size; and by freshal, that of large hoops,
which is well pressed and made to keep for a long time; but which is still newly made and still soft, in distinction from the aged, which, having been made long before being used,
has become hard.
FRICANDÓ. A dish of French
kitchen, which is regularly of shredded veal.
fricando of veal. The pulps of veal are cut into pieces two fingers thick; they are shredded with pieces of fat ham, cracked peppercorns and cloves cut into small pieces; they are put to cook in water with salt, butter,
some pieces of carrot and whole clean onions. When these and the carrots are cooked, they are browned in
butter, onion is chopped very finely,
flour is sprinkled over it, the onio[n] is fried in a little butter, and as soon as it is browned, a little of the broth
in which the meat was cooked is added to it, and it is seasoned with
all spices, except saffron and cumin; the cooked meat is then fried, it is
put into the seasoned broth, and when it has thickened greatly, it is removed and served, with the fried carrots and onions placed on top, other garnishes of fried herbs and vegetables being able to be added to it.
FRICANDO OF VEAL WITH BROTH
OF FLOUR AND CAPERS. Slices
of marbled ham are placed at the bottom of a casserole; on them are arranged slices of veal shredded with garlic, pepper, clove and cinnamon:
raw tomatoes are sliced and put
in together with whole garlic; pieces of ham are fried, and capers are ground
with a little flour and wine, so that
the broth does not remain very white;
ground clove, cinnamon and pepper are added to it, whole capers, olives
and orange or lemon leaves. Having
made this broth, enough tomatoes are chopped and put into the casserole of
the meat with a little wine; the meat is put to cook over two fires, and when it is cooked, the flour and caper broth is added to it and it is put to boil without
adding any butter. When it has thickened well, it is served.
fricando of entr[e]e. A piece of beef tongue is used, which is shredded with fine lard, and is put in a saucepan with water until it covers it, adding a piece of butter, ham scraps, salt, carrots, large whole onions, and a
leaf of laurel, and being left to cook over gentle heat for three consecutive hours. The broth is then put into a small saucepan with a burnt or roasted onion, and is left to reduce until the
degree of jelly, being thickened with this starch and the fricandó being browned in it,
the other things being placed on top, if it is to be served alone; but if it is to
be served as seasoning or sauce
for the dish of chicory, sorrel or
beef tongue, all the fricandó will be
put over the cooked herbs. The
fricandó is also served without these herbs with tomato sauce.
fricando of salmon. The
salmon is cut into slices, which are shredded and
put to cook, just like the beef tongue from the previous article,
following the same procedures until finished. It is served with tomato sauce, pepper, or Italian sauce.

pork meat, divided into small pieces, with longaniza, morcón and chicharrones, all well cooked; it is left to simmer over low heat, and when they have thickened as needed, they are set aside, and placed in the small plate, this is garnished on top with cooking oil, powdered oregano and slices of onion, avocado, pickled chili peppers and olives, radishes and lettuce hearts cut into quarters.
BRAZIL-STYLE BEANS. Tomatoes and onions are fried in lard; cloves, cinnamon, cumin, deseeded and toasted pasilla chilies, and some cooked beans with a little water are ground.
This broth is fried, then vinegar, pork ribs, fried longanizas and chorizos are added. All this is mixed with the large beans; which have been fried separately with oil, olives, chopped raw onion, a little grated or aged cheese.
LARGE BEANS WITHOUT TOMATO* A piece of bread is toasted in lard, and ground with some beans, pepper and cloves; everything is fried, then the beans with water and vinegar in equal portions and in proportion to the quantity of beans are added, and they are left to boil adding oregano and salt. When served at the table, aged cheese cut into pieces, oil, chili peppers and olives are placed on top.
CARMELITE BEANS. White large beans are put to cook with a little tequesquite, and when they are cooked, they are washed; chopped garlic cloves are fried in plenty of lard until golden, and without removing them, chile pods and chopped tomatoes are fried there as well, adding a little water and seasoning with sufficient salt; the washed beans are placed in this broth, and when they have been seasoned by boiling in it, saffron, cloves, pepper and cinnamon, all ground, onions cooked separately, boiled eggs, oil, a little vinegar, and a little parsley are added, leaving it to thicken as appropriate.
PORTUGUESE-STYLE BEANS. A good amount of tomato and onion are chopped and fried in lard, then a little bean broth with cloves, pepper, cinnamon and saffron, all ground, is added; the already cooked beans are placed there, with pork meat, also cooked, a little of the broth in which it was cooked, a little ground beans to thicken, the corresponding salt and plenty of lard and oil; they are left to thicken as appropriate and served with cheese, chili peppers and olives on top.

and the roots remain on top; on the sides of the pot wine will be introduced, mixed with the broth of the hens, in moderate quantity, throwing on the last layer burnt butter; everything is left to season over two fires, stirring from time to time with the same pot so as not to spoil the cover, which, being somewhat dry, is removed and emptied with great care into the vessel in which it is to be served.

Roasted hens in tomato broth. The hens, gutted and cleaned, are made with the tip of the knife many incisions on all parts, putting into some strips of ham, split cloves of garlic in others and in some powder of clove and pepper, covering all with small parsley leaves; thus arranged, the hens are put to cook in a pot with water and vinegar, seasoning with salt and ground saffron, and after being cooked, they are taken out of the broth, fried in butter with ground garlic; when they are well browned, they are cut, throwing into the butter roasted and ground tomatoes so that they also fry, mixing immediately the broth in which the hens were cooked, golden flour in butter, capers, capers, and when it is seasoned and has a consistent texture, olives, cured tornachiles and oil.

HENS IN YOLK BROTH. The raw hens are divided into quarters that are fried in butter with a little salt: as soon as they are, roasted and ground tomato is thrown on them, and chopped garlic and parsley, letting this seasoning macerate a little; sufficient water is then added, with clove, pepper and plenty of saffron, all ground, putting at the same time some whole poblano chiles or cuaresmeños, so that they cook in the same broth, which will be taken out as soon as they are cooked before they burst; when the hen has also been cooked, they are mixed with the broth and egg yolks, cut with vinegar, stirring much with the spoon so that no lumps form, and when it has boiled a little, the cooked chiles, oil and pieces of cauliflower also cooked are added, leaving it still to give one more boil before removing.

HUERTO DE CARNE DE PUERCO. Se
deshojan y limpian unas lechugas, y se
cuecen en agua con sal de la tierra; se
limpian y quitan los corazones á unas
zanahorias, que se pican menudas y se
ponen á cocer con una buena porción
de papas; se pican xitomates maduros,
ajos y cebollas, todo menudo, y se po-
ne á freír este xi tomate en manteca; se
sacan las lechugas y se lavan; se mon-
dan los tronquitos y se pican con las
papas y la zanahoria y se pone todo á
freír. Después se humedece con caldo
de carne de puerco, y se sazona con la
sal fina necesaria; se muele un poco de
clavo, de azafrán, pimienta y cominos,
y se echan al guisado, agregándose vina-
gre y aceite; en seguida se pone la car-
ne de puerco cocida en tajadas de lomo,
y costillitas separadas; se deja sazonar,
y cuando ya esté casi consumido el cal-
do, se apea y se sirve:
HUESITOS (Que suelen llamarse
también dátiles fingidos). Se hace al-
míbar con una libra de azúcar y un
cuartillo de miel virgen; asi que hier-
van y estén de punto alto, se añaden
media libra de avellana, media de pi-
fión, unas pocas almendras tostadas,
nuez chica, bizcocho duro cuanto baste
para espesar, un poco de clavo, de nuez
moscada y do canela, todo molido, y
ocho yemas de huevo. Asi que tenga
punto de despegar del cazo, se aparta,
y luego que se enfrie, se hacen los hue-
sitos en forma de dátiles, y se envuel-
ven en pastilla encarnada cernida.
HUEVA. Huevecillos de los pesca-
dos, que reunidos y adheridos unos á
los otros, forman una especie de masa,
comestible tanto en crudo, como sazo-
nada con especias y en tripas, que sue-
len llamarse cabial, ó molida y revuel-

HUERTO DE CARNE DE PUERCO. Lettuce leaves are removed and cleaned, and they are boiled in water with earth salt; carrots are cleaned and their cores removed, chopped finely, and put to cook with a good portion of potatoes; ripe tomatoes, garlic, and onions are chopped finely, and this tomato is fried in lard; the lettuce is removed and washed; the stalks are peeled and chopped with the potatoes and carrot, and everything is put to fry. Then it is moistened with pork broth, and seasoned with the necessary fine salt; a little clove, saffron, pepper, and cumin are ground, and added to the stew, along with vinegar and oil; then the cooked pork, sliced from the loin, and separate ribs are added; it is left to season, and when the broth is almost consumed, it is removed and served:
HUESITOS (Which are also often called false dates). A syrup is made with one pound of sugar and one quart of pure honey; once they boil and reach a high point, half a pound of hazelnuts, half a pound of pine nuts, a few roasted almonds, small nuts, hard biscuit as much as needed to thicken, a little clove, nutmeg, and cinnamon, all ground, and eight egg yolks are added. Once it has the point of peeling off the pot, it is removed, and once it has cooled, the small stones are formed into the shape of dates, and wrapped in sifted red paste.
HUEVA. Fish eggs, which, gathered and adhering to one another, form a kind of mass, edible both raw, as seasoned with spices and in intestines, which are often called cabial, or ground and mixed with chicken egg, cooked in a cake, which is stewed in escabeche.

These are fried raw in oil with garlic; once fried, they are removed and a portion of parsley, and the same amount of deflemed capers are ground; they are fried in oil, sliced onion is added, a little water is poured, and once it has thickened, the hervas are added, and when the broth is well seasoned, they are served.
Some eat them raw, mixed with oil, vinegar, pepper, salt, and parsley.

huevas de esturión. These hervas, formed into small cookies, the thickness of a finger and the size of the palm of the hand, are known by the name of cabial or Labia, which is salted and put to dry in the sun. An incredible quantity of this fish is caught at the mouth of the Volga and the other rivers that flow into the Caspian Sea, and it is also fished in the Sturgeon Lake in northern Canada. The cabial is transported up the Volga to Moscow, from where it is distributed throughout Muscovy, where it is an important resource for the Muscovites, due to the three lent periods they have in the year. A lot of cabial is also consumed in Italy, taken from the port of Arkhangelsk, and the Dutch do good business with it. The best quality is dark, reddish, and well dried, and it is eaten with oil and lemon juice.

cazuela de carpas. Estando éstas es-
camadas, vaciadas y divididas en tro-
zos, se polvorean con sal y se dejan así
una 6 dos horas para que adquieran
consistencia. Se echan entónces en el
fondo de una cazuela cuatro onzas de
mantequilla fresca, cuatro anchoas pi-
cadas y encima los trozos de carpa; se
añade media onza de polvo fino de azú-
car, una onza de alcaparras, pimienta
en grano, clavo y maclas; se cubre to-
todo con rebanadas de limón, y se echa
encima un cuartillo de vino tinto, y otro
tanto de vinagre, y se cubre la cazuela
herméticamente, tapando las junturas
con engrudo ó con pasta de harina de
arroz, 6 con masa de maiz; se deja cocer
á fuego suave y se sirve de entrada en
la misma cazuela.

pio de nuestros países calientes, cuya
carne y huevos son buenos de comer.

cazón (véase CAZON, pág. 162). Tam-
bién suele comerse en caldillo de xito-
mate ó tomate con chile verde (véase
ENTOMATADO, pág. 310).

el artículo anterior).

IBEX. A species of wild goat,
with large horns, which increase each year until they reach twenty
knots. It is also called Rupicabra.
Its meat is prepared and cooked in the same way as that of the roe deer (see ROE DEER,
pages 229 and 230).
ICHUSS ET-K ARPFEN. A German
table entry, equivalent to
carp casserole. When these are
scaled, gutted and divided into pieces, they are dusted with salt and left thus
for one or two hours to acquire
consistency. Then four ounces of
fresh butter, four chopped anchovies and on top the pieces of carp; add half an ounce of fine sugar powder, one ounce of capers, pepper
corns, cloves and macis; cover to-
tally with lemon slices, and pour
on a quart of red wine, and the same amount of vinegar, and cover the casserole
hermetically, sealing the joints
with paste or with rice flour paste, or with corn dough; let it cook
over low heat and serve as an entry
in the same casserole.
IGUANA. A species of lizard, native to our hot countries, whose
meat and eggs are good to eat.
It is prepared and cooked in the same way as the dogfish (see DOGFISH, p. 162). It is also commonly eaten in broth of xito-
mate or tomato with green chili (see TOMATO SOUP, p. 310).
IGUARACU. A species of crocodile,
native to our country and to Brazil, also edible, which is prepared and seasoned in the same way as the iguana (see the
previous article).

JAMON EN VINO A LA FRANCESA. Des-
pues de remojado el jamón por tres días
en agua fria, se deja escurrir, y envuel-
to en un lienzo blanco y limpio, se po
ne á cocer en partes iguales de vino y
agua con zanahorias, cebollas, tomillo,
laurel, clavo y un manojito de yerbas
finas.
Se conoce que está bien cocido, si se
puede atravesar fácilmente con una a-
guja de mechar. Después de cocido se
le quita el hueso de enmedio, y estando
enteramente frío, se levanta la tapa, que
se vuelve á cubrir con grasa, raspadu-
ra de pan y yerbas finas.
JAMON EN VINO, MECHADO. Se lim-
pia el jamón y se mecha con canela,
clavo y pimienta entera, poniéndose en
una olla á cocer con una poca de agua
y otro tanto de vino. Se tapa la olla, y
estando cocido el jamón, se saca y se
despelleja; se le echa por encima polvo
grueso de azúcar, que se quema con
planchas bien calientes, y se espolvorea
después con mas azúcar, clavo y cane-
la, todo molido.

MANÁ. For nine quarts of
milk, half a cup of peeled and ground chickpeas, half a cup of pine nuts and half a cup of small nuts; these and the pine nuts are put in warm water and their skin is removed; one cup of raw rice,
four ounces of almonds (all this ground and the almonds sliced), strips of cinnamon and whole cloves, a lemon peel and orange leaves, nine egg yolks, some grains of
salt: a syrup is made that is placed on the fire and stirred, and once
it is halfway done, the almonds, nuts and pine nuts are added; once it pulls away from the pot, it is poured into a platter, and
left from one day to the next; powdered sugar and cinnamon are sprinkled on top

over fire so that it forms a crust.
MANATÍ. The manatee or lamantino
as others call it, although it resembles the shark in shape, is of a very different nature and of larger size, since
there is an author who says that in our seas manatees have been caught so large that to transport one of them it
was necessary to use a cart with two
teams of oxen. It is viviparous like
the dolphin; but the female gives birth to only one at a time, although of enormous
volume. Some authors place it in the class of amphibians, which is an
error, because it does not live on land and only
takes its head and part of its body out of the water to reach the herbs
on the banks of rivers, where it is usually found, although properly speaking it is
marine. Its meat is tasty and delicate and similar to that of veal, like that of the shark, and it is prepared and seasoned
in the same way as its last (see SHARK, page 162).

FISH).
fried mojarras. After being
gutted, scaled and well cleaned, they are dried after being washed, they are well coated
inside with flour, and they are rolled
outside in the same; they are fried immediately in oil and butter or in butter alone and they are served.
MOJARRAS WITH PARSLEY AND TOMATO.
After the mojarras are cleaned and scaled,
raw garlic is ground, and it is
dissolved in oil; fresh parsley is ground and a lemon is squeezed from it; salt and a little pepper are added, everything ground in such a way that it forms a thick sauce: the mojarras are smeared with it
inside and outside, they are wrapped in
papers coated with oil; they are placed
on the grill and over gentle heat they are left
to cook; when they are done, the paper is removed from them. A pot is placed on the fire; oil is added and cooked tomato, well ground, is fried, enough sliced onion, green chili without skin very finely chopped, and when everything is well fried, the mojarras are added and placed over very gentle heat; a little watery vinegar is added, and when the broth has been consumed, oil is added to them and they are left to rest over heat for a long
time, served with parsley and chopped onion on top. It is very well
possible to put xitomate instead of tomato, or
to make a mixture of both things.
MOJARRAS IN ESCABECHE. After
the mojarras are well cleaned, they are dried and rolled in flour; ancho chilies are toasted without veins without burning,
so that they become very dry and can be made into powder. A paste is formed from oil, roasted garlic and toasted cumin, it is thinned with a little vinegar, the mojarras are smeared with it
inside and outside, and then the chili powder is sprinkled all over them.
A paste is formed with a little flour, two or three egg yolks, sufficient salt and a little oil; everything is well mixed by stirring, until
taken with a spoon it forms a thread
when poured out; the mojarras are bathed in this broth and fried in butter until
they are well browned.

With this mixture the thick intestines of the pig are stuffed, which will have been cleaned well, without removing the fat; they are tied to leave the morcones of the size that is desired and they are put to boil in boiling water. They are eaten fried or grilled on the grill with a good chili sauce, or with another proper one if wine is to be drunk over them.

MORCONES OR BLOOD SAUSAGES FOR GIFTING.

A pot is prepared with onion, garlic, tomato, parsley, clove, pepper, cinnamon and deseeded and toasted ancho chiles, all ground; thyme, in powder if it is dry, or chopped if fresh, pieces of finely chopped pig intestine, raisins, split almonds and pine nuts, seasoning everything with the necessary salt. Over this mixture the pig’s blood is received, which will be stirred well with it before it cools, so that everything is well incorporated; more salt is added if it lacks it, and with this mixture the pig’s intestines are stuffed after being well washed, prepared with salt and lemon slices and rinsed afterwards; they are tied at the appropriate distance according to the size that the morcones or blood sausages are desired, which are then put to boil in boiling water.

SIMPLE MORCONES WITH ANISE, CUMIN AND CILANTRO. The pot is prepared with salt, garlic, anise, cumin and toasted and ground cilantro: the pig’s blood is received in it and in the rest one proceeds as in the previous article.

MORCONES WITH TOMATO, MINT AND LIME PEEL. The pot is prepared with garlic, onions, tomatoes, tomatoes, parsley, mint, thyme, fresh oregano and lime peel, all finely chopped; it is seasoned with salt and the pig’s blood is received on top, so that one proceeds in the rest as in the previous articles.

FRENCH-STYLE MORCONES AND BLOOD SAUSAGES (see black pudding, page 88 and wild boar pudding, page 89).

TURKEY MORCONES. A pot is prepared with the same mixture that was said for the gifting morcones (see above); but in less quantity, which must be proportional to the blood of one turkey.

PAMPANO RELLENO DE OTRO MODO.
Después de desalado el rámpano, se pi-
ca xitomate crudo quitadas las pepitas;
se pica cebolla menuda y njo, se agre-
gan papas y almendras picadas, peregil
y alcaparras; se frie todo mucho en
manteca, se echa uu poco de vinagre
aguado y un trozo de azúcar. Así que
se ha sazonado formando una masa es-
peso, se rellena el pescado; se pone un
papel en el fondo de una cazuela, se
echa aceite, se unta el pescado también
con aceite, se pone á dos fuegos hasta
que está cocido, y quitándole el aceite
en que se coció, se unta con limón y
se vuelve á poner con el papel hasta
que se dore por uno y otro lado. Des-
pués se guisa en algún caldillo, 6 se
sirve con una de las salsas dichas en el
artículo anterior.
PAMPANOS RELLENOS DE CHICHAROS.
Se frien en manteca chícharos y exotes
cocidos, picados los segundos con cebo-
llas, ajos y xitomates crudos, todo muy
menudo, sazonándose con sal, clavo y
pimienta molida; estando rendido el re-
cado, se lo echan huevos á medio batir,
y estando todo cuajado, se rellenan con
este picadillo los pámpanos después de
limpios y desalados; se atan con un hi-
lo y se envuelven en papeles bien en-
mantecados, poniéndose en seguida á
asar en la parrilla y cuidándose de vol-
tearlos de uno y otro lado; estando co-
cidos, se les quitan los papeles, se de-
satan y se sirven de este modo, ó revol-
cados en harina y vueltos á freir, ador-
nándose con alcaparras, chililos y acei-
tunas.

Well deboned, it is stuffed with the prepared dough, salt and pepper are added to it, it is smeared with oil on top, a powder of dried chili, ground and sifted, is added to it, it is wrapped in an oiled paper and put to fry in oil with garlic; it is served with some of the sauces for fish (see FISH).
PAMPANO STUFFED IN ANOTHER WAY.
After the pámpano has been desalted, raw tomato is chopped, the seeds removed; finely chopped onion and garlic are chopped, potatoes and chopped almonds are added, parsley and capers; everything is fried a lot in butter, a little watered vinegar and a piece of sugar are added. As soon as it has been seasoned forming a thick mass, the fish is stuffed; a paper is placed at the bottom of a casserole, oil is added, the fish is also smeared with oil, it is put over two fires until it is cooked, and removing the oil in which it was cooked, it is smeared with lemon and put back with the paper until it browns on one and the other side. Afterward it is cooked in some broth, or it is served with one of the sauces mentioned in the previous article.
PAMPANOS STUFFED WITH PEAS.
Peas and cooked pods are fried in butter, the latter chopped with onions, garlic and raw tomatoes, all very finely, seasoned with salt, clove and ground pepper; when the seasoning is tender, beaten eggs are added to it, and when everything is set, the pámpanos are stuffed with this chopped mixture after being cleaned and desalted; they are tied with a string and wrapped in well-buttered papers, then put to roast on the grill and taking care to turn them from one side and the other; when cooked, the papers are removed from them, they are untied and served in this way, or rolled in flour and fried again, garnished with capers, chilies and olives.

PAPA 6 POTATO. Plant native to southern America, which today
is already cultivated throughout Europe, where
they have learned from us the use of the
bulbs of its root, eating them prepared in different ways. We
call them generally potatoes and the
Spaniards potatoes, and although there are at least
eleven varieties of them, which are
distinguished by the color of the skin or
shell that covers them, by their shape and
by the color of the pulp, which in some is
more yellowish than in others, all are
edible and are prepared and seasoned in the same way, although some, such as the white, round and flattened, are more tasty and delicate than
the others. With them is also made a
pleasant and healthy bread, and it is extracted from
them the nutritious starch so useful in
innumerable cases (see STARCH,
page 334).
FRIED POTATOES - The potatoes are cooked,
either by putting them in water and putting them on
the fire until they boil well, or by putting them in a pot with a little water, covering the mouth with a cloth, and then with
a lid or vessel well fitted; of
this way they lose nothing of substance a) when cooking. Cooked in any
way, they are peeled, sliced and fried
in lard or butter, adding the
corresponding salt, and when they are
already about to brown, they are served alone, or with
salt and pepper, or accompanied by some sauce, such as those of chili or of xito-
mate.
POTATOES IN SPICE. Cooked potatoes, they are sliced; then a
little xitomate and soaked bread is ground; a casserole is placed with lard on the fire, a few chopped
garlics are fried in it and then the ground xitomate.
Two or three onions divided into quarters, whole green chilies
and a little chopped parsley are added to it, the
necessary fine salt is added, and then the
chopped potatoes and some shrimp, or cooked pieces of pork meat with the water in which they were cooked; they must boil over strong fire, and when the broth has thickened a little,
cloves and pepper with a few
cumin seeds and saffron, all ground; thus that the broth has been well seasoned and thickened, they can be served at the
table.
POTATOES WITH CHEESE. The
raw potatoes are peeled, sliced, and then
ripe tomatoes, garlic
and a little of all spices are ground separately; a bed of potatoes is placed in a baking dish, another of grated cheese, another of the ground
spices, and the beds are alternated until the casserole is filled; when it is full, it will be placed over two gentle fires until the potatoes are cooked, which
are served with chopped parsley on top.
POTATOES STEWED WITH OIL. Small chopped tomatoes, tomatoes, onions and green poblano chiles without veins,
and they are put to fry in plenty of lard; while doing so, a little flour is added, and it is stirred so that the sauce does not remain either
thick or watery; then the large sliced potatoes are added, plenty of oil and a powder of Tabasco pepper; thus that they have boiled a little, a little good vinegar is added,
they are left to season and then they are put to
rest over the steam of a pot.
POTATOES (Toasted). The potatoes are put to cook in the embers; once cooked,
they are peeled and ground with a few
creams, they are passed through a sieve and butter, chopped parsley and
some beaten eggs are added to them; some balls are formed on ground bread, they are fried
later and sugar and orange blossom water are added to them.
SOUND POTATOES. Cooked and peeled-

covered with another layer of dough flattened
as mentioned before, and it is covered again
with the comal with fire.

Formados los pastel illos como los del
artículo anterior, se rellenan con un picadillo de ave cocida, grasa, ubre de

remojado en crema, cebollas, sal y pimienta, todo picado y mezclado, y ligado con cinco yernos de huevo. Después de concluidos y dorados los paste-

ve entonces á poner en los pastel illos,
pudiéndose hacer esta operación con
crema y yemas de huevo á falta de caldo-colado.

común.

Everything is left to season, and when it has thickened as usual, it is set aside.

It is left to season well, and when served, cooking oil, olives, capers, chilitos in vinegar and sesame seeds are added to them.

After the ducks are skinned and the rump removed, they are put in an infusion of water with tequesquite and onion tails for eight or ten hours; they are then put to cook in water with salt and two whole onions. When cooked, they are set aside and a little of the blood sausage filling with toasted bread and cooked lettuces is ground. A casserole is put on the fire with equal amounts of lard and oil, some clean garlic cloves are browned there, the ground mixture is fried and broth from that in which the duck was cooked is added to it.

excerpts.translation:
SMAS TO THE BURGESE. If one wishes to make Spanish sauce, a light red substance will be made, which is seasoned with the same broth in which the partridges were stewed; it is passed through a silk sieve, allowed to reduce until it is reduced by half so that it takes on a good flavor, it is degreased, passed through the worsted, and poured over the partridges.

Partridges Mexican-style. Fried in butter are garlic and parsley chopped, thin slices of onion and roasted and ground tomatoes; when this is done, pepper, cloves, cumin, and toasted bread fried in butter, all ground, oregano, salt, vinegar, broth from the same in which the partridges were cooked and capers are added; in this broth the partridges already cooked and fried in butter with ground garlic are placed, and they are left to boil until the dish is seasoned and in good consistency. When removed, olives, cured tornachiles, and raw [illegible] are added.

Roasted partridges on the grill. After cleaning, they are placed raw on the grill, turning them with oil; they are rolled in breadcrumbs and returned to the grill to brown; they are served with lettuce salad without chopping.

excerpts.translation: o fried, where the cooked or boiled fish will be put to boil with the necessary salt. When removed from the heat, oil and vinegar are added to it. FISH IN EMPIADA BROTH. 2 fried tomatoes and chopped onions with a little ground saffron; it is poured over the raw fish, adding chopped parsley, ground pepper, oil, salt, and a little water; it is covered and cooked over fire until the fish is well cooked. This broth is varied; it is also made with tomato and garlic paste, and after adding a little clove and pepper. MARINATED FISH. A few cloves of garlic are fried in butter, they are removed and two parts of vinegar and one part of wine are poured in, adding fine pepper and coarse pepper, clove and cumin, all ground with bay leaves and dried oregano. The fish is left there in infusion for some time, and when cold, the sauce is poured over it and it is served. FISH IN FLOUR BROTH. After roasting or boiling the fish, onions and garlic finely chopped and pepper are fried in butter; a little flour is browned, and dissolved with a little water, it is added to the onion and before taking the fish to the table, the broth is poured over it. FISH IN FLOUR BROTH WITH green chili. Onions, tomatoes, garlic, green chilies, parsley, and good herbs are chopped and fried in butter; a little flour is also fried and browned and stirred with the fried seasoning. A little of the broth in which the fish was cooked is added to everything, if it is to be served boiled, and chopped capers; but if said fish is to be served roasted or fried, no water is added, and in both cases small amounts of vinegar are gradually added. This sauce or broth is poured over the fish to take to the table. FRIED FISH (Sauce for). Flour is browned in butter with a little garlic and quite a bit of very finely chopped onion; some raw tomatoes are squeezed there, and when everything is well fried, oil and quite a bit of water are added, letting it boil until the broth is regularly thick. Then it is removed from the heat and the already fried fish with flour in butter, chopped parsley, and cooked onion are put in the broth. FISH IN TOMATO BROTH with tomatoes. Tomato with chopped garlic is fried: separately, onion is fried with tomatoes; everything is combined and spices are added without forgetting saffron, capers, pitted raisins, almonds, small chilies, fish broth, oil, vinegar, oregano, and toasted sesame seeds. FISH WITH GARLIC-CUMIN. Some cloves of roasted garlic are ground with cumin, they are thinned with a little water with salt, and oil, vinegar, oregano, and ground pepper are added to them. The fresh fish is put there, and it is left to cook over two fires, taking care to turn it from time to time so that it cooks evenly.

same herbs, fried garlic and some lime peels; the pot is covered and left to rest for three or four days, in which the white fish will already be in good condition to eat. They are served with oil, vinegar, chopped onion and powdered oregano, adorned with olives, cured tornachiles and capers. They can also be served after draining, on a salad of lettuce or endive, composed with oil, vinegar, salt, roasted and ground tomatoes and chopped onion, adorned with chilies and olives.

WHITE FISH, STEWED WITH TOMATO, CAPERS AND FLOUR. Some roasted and ground tomatoes are fried in oil with garlic, adding after frying, chopped parsley, capers, cooked onions, ground pepper, salt and golden flour, thinned with water from the same in which the onions were cooked; when the broth is well seasoned and before it thickens, the cleaned white fish are put in it to cook. To serve, oil is poured over them and they are adorned with capers, chilies and olives.

WHITE FISH IN TOMATO BROTH. Garlic and tomatoes are crushed, and mixed with soaked bread, well ground, the fish are put to cook there with vinegar, pepper, coriander, oregano, pieces of onion and cooked chilies. At the time of serving, oil is added to them.

WHITE FISH STUFFED WITH EGG. Onion and chopped tomato are fried in butter; a little water is added, ground spices of all kinds and salt; beaten egg is then added and everything is stirred so that it remains like scrambled eggs, and it is fried together; olives, chopped chilies and small pieces of hard-boiled egg are added, and with this mixture the fish will be stuffed, which will have been kept very clean and ready. They are closed, and covered with beaten egg, they are fried. They are served thus, or in broth, which is made by frying garlic, onion and tomato, all chopped; it is thickened with bread fried in butter and spices of all kinds are added.

WHITE FISH STUFFED AND PAPER-WRAPPED. Eggs are boiled and the yolks are removed, which are mixed with chopped parsley and ground pepper, the whites being chopped; with this the fish are stuffed, which will have been already gutted and very washed with cold water. Sheets of paper are spread on a table, and on them breadcrumbs are poured, mixed with chopped parsley and ground pepper; the fish are placed in a row, as many as fit in each sheet; the same breadcrumbs, parsley and pepper are poured over them; they are sprinkled with plenty of oil, and the sheets are folded on the four sides so that they do not drain.

PICHON. The pigeon. Its
meat is of a delicate taste, succulent, nutritious, easy to digest and it is
prepared and seasoned in innumerable
ways, of which the main ones are those that include the following articles.
PICHONES EMPAPELADOS A LA MEXICANA. Put oregano to boil in
a little water and when it comes to a boil, remove it. Put to fry in a casserole
quite a few tomatoes with onions and parsley, all chopped very finely, slices
of ham and a sprig of thyme;
when well fried, add the oregano water, a little breadcrumbs, powdered, toasted coriander, saffron, cloves,
cinnamon and pepper, all ground; stir well with the oregano broth,
and let it boil until it thickens considerably. Coat the raw pigeons with this frying mixture, and once well covered, roll them in breadcrumbs or toasted and ground breadcrumbs, and place them in papers greased with butter, with
sufficient salt; wrap them well without leaving anything but the legs outside.

GREEN. When the pumpkin seeds are well dried, they are rubbed with a coarse ayate or cotence cloth to remove the outer fuzz; they are then soaked in salt water for a while and afterwards sun-dried so that they dry again; in that case they are ground with a fire-lit cajete under the metate, like cacao, until the paste becomes very smooth; they are then fried in fat until small balls form, and then cumin, garlic, chilies, and tomatoes are added, all raw and ground; after this is fried and seasoned with salt, the gnaxolote, chicken <fcc. divided into regular portions, with the broth in which it was cooked, is added, and left to boil until the pipian or mole becomes thick. The quantity of chilies varies according to taste, since some want the dishes spicier than others.

CHICKEN IN CILANTRO STEW. Two parts of dried cilantro and

until the butter rises to the top and it is set aside; green chile, xito-
mate, tomato, and garlic are fried separately, everything chopped very

of the chickens is added, sufficient salt, clove, cinnamon, pepper, and toasted bread fried in

and onions cooked separately are added; when the broth has
thickened, it is set aside and left to rest.
CHICKEN IN MUD. Some ancho chiles are veined and washed well, and
they are ground with ripe xitomates; separately, four tablets of chocolate, and a little cinnamon and clove are ground; this is combined with the ground xitomate and raisins, almonds, and pine nuts, toasted sesame, and sufficient salt are added; this broth is increased with the necessary water and everything is put in a pot brushed
with butter. The raw chickens are fried in butter, they are added to the broth and
put over two gentle fires until
they are cooked, taking care to stir them with the same pot from time to time.
MULATTO CHICKEN. After the chickens are cooked, they are shredded with toasted almonds and fried in oil; hazelnuts, gizzards, and a little
biscuit are ground; this is dissolved in a part of the broth of the chickens and another of wine,
it is seasoned with ground clove, cinnamon, and pepper, and sufficient salt, and the chickens are put to boil in this broth until it thickens.

CHICKEN IN BEET AND
LETTUCE BROTH. As in the previous article, with the difference that the beet
will not be ground but chopped and that instead of apple, lettuce will be used, also chopped as for salad.
To serve, sprinkle toasted sesame seeds on top.
CHICKEN IN PINE NUT BROTH. Grind together roasted pine nuts and tomatos, and fry in lard with
salt; then add cloves, cinnamon
and pepper, all ground, wine, the broth
of the chickens and a little vinegar; in
this broth the cooked chickens are placed
and left to boil until everything is well seasoned.
CHICKEN IN BROTH OF WINE AND
ORANGE. Fry the raw chickens in
lard and then add wine and
orange juice, a lump of sugar,
raisins, almonds and pine nuts, ground cloves and cinnamon; let them cook in this
broth, which is thickened afterwards with fried and ground toast.
CHICKEN IN TOMATO SAUCE. Fry in burnt lard some chopped garlic cloves and then cooked and ground tomatoes with cloves, pepper and cinnamon; place in this frying the chickens
with their broth, sliced chorizo, raisins,
almonds, cooked and chopped beet with
parsley, fried and ground bread and white wine; let them boil, taking care that
the broth does not become too clear.
SHREDDED CHICKEN. Shred with strips of ham, split garlic, spice cloves
and small pieces of cinnamon, and fry
in a pot with plenty of lard and
the necessary salt; then fry in the
same roasted and ground tomatos with
cloves, toasted coriander and saffron, add plenty of [illegible] chopped parsley, water, vinegar, almonds and capers and put the chickens to cook in this broth, adding when they are [illegible] olives and
cured chiles.
CHICKEN IN COOKED AND MIXED SALAD. Fry in lard finely chopped garlic and
onions, roasted and ground tomatos and strips or slices of roasted and peeled green chile; when this seasoning is half fried or tender, season with salt, cloves, pepper, saffron,
cumin and parsley, all ground, and add lettuce, cauliflower, and artichokes,
all cooked and chopped, olives and capers; place the cooked chickens there,
divided into quarters and fried, and add vinegar and a little of their broth so that they may boil; let the broth reduce, remove and let rest before serving.

soup of tripe. The tripe is first cleaned very well, whether of sheep or cow, and is perfectly cooked in water with salt; they are finely chopped with butter, garlic, and roasted and ground tomatoes; the tripe cut into small pieces is then added, saffron, cumin, toasted coriander, cloves, and pepper, all ground, and a little of the broth in which the tripe was cooked; it is left to boil, and when it is somewhat dry, it is set aside, and in another buttered casserole, a layer of fried and golden bread slices is placed, and another layer of small pieces of tripe already prepared as stated, sprinkled with grated cheese and a little pepper, and alternating thus the layers until concluding with a layer of bread; the remaining broth of the tripe, or the amount needed to make the soup, is then poured, which, once cooked, is set aside, covered with breadcrumbs, brushed with burnt butter, covered with a comal with fire to brown, and served with parsley leaves on top.

jas de maiz bien escurridas, y se podran

muy poca manteca y mas azúcar, de cuya masa se forman unas rosquillas mas
ó menos grandes que se meten á cocer
al horno sobre hojas de lata. Su bajo
precio hace que se consuman muchas
cantidades en esta forma ó en la de co-
chi nitos por los muchachos.
TAPADO. Guisado hecho con rebanadas de x i tomate, y con otras verduras y legumbres, con las que se tapan
las carnes de toda clase y se ponen á
cocer á dos fuegos. En los artículos
respectivos á cada una de las carnes 6
legumbres, se explica el modo de disponer el tapado, pudiendo por ejemplo
verse los siguientes.
Tapado de carne de cerdo pág. 175.

TAPAR HERMETICAMENTE.
Se entiende en la cocina por esta expresión, tapar una olla 6 vasija cualquiera
con un lienzo y un plato 6 cazuela encima, ó con sola una cazuela, engru-
dando las junturas, de modo que al
hervir lo que contiene, no pueda esca
parse el vapor.

veal (Salpicon of). The pulp of veal is boiled well with interveined ham in large pieces, and salt; after both things are well cooked, they are shredded by mixing them; they are placed on the plate, chopped onion, salt, pepper, capers, chopped parsley, onion and avocado in slices, oil and vinegar as for salad are poured over them, and it is garnished on top with olives and chilies in vinegar.
veal (Salpicon of) in xitomate sauce. Well cooked the pulp of veal, it is shredded and seasoned with the following sauce: roasted xitomates are ground in sufficient quantity, and finely chopped onions, oregano, vinegar, plenty of oil, pitted olives in halves, chopped chilies in vinegar, slices of roasted poblano or Lenten chiles, and capers are added to them; everything is incorporated with the shredded meat and placed on a plate, garnished on top with other whole olives, cured tornachiles and capers.
veal (Fried liver of). Butter or lard is melted in a pan, and the liver cut into pieces, dusted with flour, is fried there; once fried, they are moistened with some mutton broth and some white wine, salt, allspice and finely chopped herbs are added to them, and they are left to cook; when they are done, they are served.

veal (Oxtails 6). After the oxtails are very clean, they are put to cook with salt, and when they are well cooked, they are deboned and cut into regular pieces. A pot is put on the fire with butter, a sufficient quantity of tomatoes are crushed on the metate, they are put in water and washed well; then green chiles, some sprigs of culantro and a few cumin seeds are ground; all this is fried in the butter and moistened with water: salt is added and it is left to season and for the broth to thicken, and they are served.

veal (Mole of Cecina 6 Ribs). From the previous day, the meat is put to desalt, and on the day it is to be cooked, it is boiled on strong fire: when it has been well cooked, it is removed; a little pasilla chile and another mulato chile are deseeded, they are toasted very well without burning, and then they are ground with a few cooked tomatoes and a few cloves for eating, the ground mixture is fried in butter and moistened with cecina broth; salt is added, the meat is cut into regular pieces, it is put in the clemole adding some small sprigs of epazote, and it is left to boil until the broth has thickened as usual. The cecina is prepared and cooked in the same way, which remains very tasty in this clemole, and particularly the udder and the chest of veal or cow.

cinnamon; the ground mixture is fried in lard and seasoned
with salt, then the meats to be cooked are added with the broth
in which they were boiled, and left to boil
until they have a good consistency.
The chickens are very good
in this clemole.
TLEMOLE OF EPAZOTE FOR CECINA,
chicharrón or chito. Soaked and
well cleaned cecina is put to half-cook in water with salt, lard and epazote; when it is, ancho chiles and pasillas and sesame are fried in lard, all
toasted and ground together with cooked tomatoes; once everything is well fried, the pot of cecina is poured in, which
is left to finish cooking at the same time that the broth thickens.
Chicharrón and chito are added to
this clemole without being cooked separately.
One can also make it with pork meat, following the same procedures as for cooking, and one can finally omit the sesame, and add small zucchini.

and other dishes.

capon, boiled in water with salt, is stuffed with
a mixture made as follows: chopped or sliced longaniza or sausage after being cooked, and it is
fried in lard with salt, garlic, onions

all the things previously mentioned; a casserole is greased with lard, a little
beaten egg is poured into it, and a layer of picadillo is placed and another of chopped vegetables with the little hands and the tongue, covered with pine nuts, raisins and
almonds; another layer of picadillo is added, and they are alternated in the order indicated until the casserole is filled,
which is covered with more beaten egg, and
the cake is set to cook at two gentle fires. It is served with fried tomato sauce, which they call de Ángeles, adding small chilies, olives and sliced hard-boiled eggs.
PEAR CAKE. The pears are chopped or sliced; they are lightly fried in
lard and set aside; a casserole is greased with lard, a little
beaten egg is poured into it, and a layer of half-fried pear is placed, another of thinly sliced tomatoes and onions and another of boiled chicken quarters,
with also boiled chorizo, filling the gaps with raisins, almonds, pieces of ham, cured tornachiles and olives; another layer of pear is added, and the others are alternated in the order indicated,
longaniza or sausage after the seasoning has been sautéed in the lard,
and adding beaten eggs so that
by setting and drying, the mixture is formed, to which are added raisins, almonds, olives, capers and pieces of ham.

One pound of rice, cleaned and soaked, is ground, and it is cooked with six [illegible] of milk, strained through a sieve with the necessary sugar, until the consistency of blancmange; half a pound of minced pork loin is cooked, and then it is minced again, immediately put into fat in which some cloves of garlic have been fried, with a [illegible] of water, ground cinnamon and clove, [illegible] covered, pine nuts, raisins, almonds, and the bread that is needed to form a paste; a tart pan is greased with fat, it is sprinkled with ground bread, a layer of the milk mixture mentioned at the beginning is placed, it is also sprinkled with ground bread, another layer of minced meat is placed, which is sprinkled likewise; and in this order more is placed until there are three [layers of] minced meat and four of milk, the latter being the last, which will be covered with bread; the tart is put to cook over gentle fires or in the oven, and when it has set, ground sugar and cinnamon are poured over it.

truchas (Pastel de). Se mechan es-
tas con tiras de anguilas y de anchoas.
Se dispone con ellas el pastel y se un-
ta con mantequilla fresca; se hace un
guisado con carne de trucha, hongos,
criadillas de tierra, perejil, cebollitas,
mantequilla fresca, yerbas {inas, espe-
cias, sal y pimienta, se echa sobre* las
truchas y se cubre con mas mantequi-
lla, concluyéndose la operación del mo-
do común; se pone á cocer el pastel,
que se desengrasa después de cocido, se
le echa un guiso <le cangrejos y se sir-
ve caliente.
trucha (Pastelitos de). Estando co-
cida la trucha, se prepara su carne lo
mismo que la de rodaballo para croque-
tas, (véase croquetas de rombo ó ro-
daballo, pág. 244), aumentando la
salsa para que esté un poco mas líqui-
da; se hacen los timbales de masa y se
echa en ellos el guiso.
trucha (Tiras saltadas de). Se sa-
can las tiras de las truchas, se prepa-
ran, se les quita en seguida el pellejo
del lado de las escamas y so cortan las
tiras en pequeñas piezas, del tamaño de
una peseta ó mas chicas, disponiéndo-
se de modo que todas queden - del mis-
mo largo y del mismo grueso; se aco-
modan en una cacerola de saltar, y se
siembran de perejil picado muy fino y
bien lavado, de sal, pimienta gorda y
raspadura de nuez moscada; se derrite
un trozo de mantequilla que se echa so-
bre las tiras de trucha, y al momento
de servirse, se fríen saltándose á fue-
go ardiente; estando doradas ó crespas
de un lado, se voltean, no dejándolas
mas que un instante sobre el fuego; se
ftderezan amontonadas al rededor de
un plato, poniéndose las restantes en
medio y echándoles salsa italiana gor-
da 6 magra. (Véase ITALIANA, pág.
430).
TROCHAS RELLENAS A LA FRANCE-
SA. Se vacian y lavan cuatro truchas
pequeñas de igual tamaño, se dejan es-
currir y se rellenan con un compuesto
de quenelles de carpa, trufas cortadas
en forma de grandes dados, y hongos;
se les atan las cabezas y se ponen á co-
cer en caldillo ligero, como se ha di-
cho en uno de los artículos anteriores;
concluido su cocimiento, se dejan en-
friar, se escurren, se revuelcan dos ve-
ces en pan rallado, rebozándose en ca-
da una con huevos batidos, y al mo-
mento de servirlas se frien, haciéndose
que se pongan de un hermoso color; se
aderezan en un plato sobre salsa de xi-
tomate á la francesa. (Véase en la pég.
778.)
TRUCHA A LA CHAMBORD. Estando
ya vacia, se calienta metiéndose en
agua hirviendo; se le quitan perfecta-
mente todos los pellejos, se lava muy
bien en muchas aguas, se deja escurrir
y se mecha con clavos gruesos de tru-
fas en forma de dominó; se pone á co-
cer en una buena marinada de vino, y
al momento de servirse, se escune y se
adereza en un plato ovalado ó pescade-
ra, guarneciéndola con cuatro molle-
juelas de ternera mechadas, cuatro pi-
chones cocidos, ocho quenelles con zu-
mo de naranja ágria, y ocho buenos
cangrejos; se le echa finalmente en lu-
gar de salsa un buen guisado á la fi-
nanciera (véase FINANCIERA).
trucha frita. Se siguen los mis-
mos procedimientos indicados para la
carpa (véase carpa frita, pág. 160).

pia la trucha, se divide en trozos que

trout (Trout Pie). These are butterflied with strips of eels and anchovies.
The pie is arranged with them and brushed with fresh butter; a stew is made with trout meat, mushrooms,
sweetbreads, parsley, spring onions,
fresh butter, herbs [illegible], spices, salt and pepper, it is poured over the
trout and covered with more butter, concluding the operation in the usual manner; the pie is put to cook,
which is skimmed after cooking, a
stew of crabs is poured over it and it is served hot.
trout (Small Trout Pies). When the trout is cooked, its meat is prepared
just like that of turbot for croquettes, (see croquettes of turbot or turbot, p. 244), increasing the
sauce so that it is a little more liquid; pastry cases are made and the stew is poured into them.
trout (Sautéed Trout Strips). The strips are taken from the trout, they are prepared, the skin is immediately removed from the scale side and the
strips are cut into small pieces, the size of
a peseta or smaller, arranged so that all end up of the same length and the same thickness; they are placed in a sauté pan, and
they are sprinkled with very finely chopped and
well-washed parsley, salt, allspice and
grated nutmeg; a piece of butter is melted which is poured over the trout strips, and at the
moment of serving, they are fried sautéing over high heat; when golden or crisp
on one side, they are turned, not leaving them
more than an instant on the fire; they
are dressed piled around
a dish, placing the remaining ones in
the middle and pouring over them thick or thin Italian sauce. (See ITALIAN, p.
430).
STUFFED TROUT FRENCH STYLE. Four small trout of equal size are emptied and washed, they are left to drain and are stuffed with a mixture of carp meatballs, truffles cut
in the shape of large cubes, and mushrooms;
their heads are tied and they are put to cook in light broth, as has been said in one of the previous articles;
when their cooking is finished, they are left to cool, they are drained, they are rolled twice in breadcrumbs, coating each one with beaten eggs, and at the moment of serving them they are fried, making
sure they turn a beautiful color; they
are dressed on a dish with French-style tomato
sauce. (See on p.
778.)
TROUT CHAMBORD STYLE. When
already emptied, it is heated by putting it in
boiling water; all the skins are perfectly removed, it is washed very
well in many waters, it is left to drain
and it is butterflied with large truffle cloves in domino shape; it is put to cook in a good wine marinade, and
at the moment of serving, it is drained and
dressed on an oval dish or fish platter, garnishing it with four sweetbreads of veal butterflied, four cooked squabs, eight meatballs with juice of sour orange, and eight good
crabs; finally, instead of sauce, a good stew French-style (see FRENCH-STYLE) is poured over it.

Well-prepared ribs are tossed with a little butter,
a head of garlic and some shallots
until they are well fried on both
sides; the fire is then moderated, the tossing pan is covered, fire is placed on top and the ribs are left to simmer gently for a quarter of an hour; the ribs are then removed and a little meat gelatin and tomato sauce are poured into the tossing pan, and left to thicken; the ribs are placed in this gelatin, gently boiled for a few minutes and served over macaroni à la napolitana (see page 491.)
beef (Square of) roasted. In the article Beef Square à la bourgeoise, page 929, one can see what is meant by beef square, and once this is well prepared, it is pierced with a thick skewer and laid on the spit so as not to pierce the tenderloin.
beef (Square of) larded and jellied. Once this piece is conveniently prepared, and the tenderloin freed from the skins and nerves that cover it, it is larded with fine or thin lard; then it is tied so as not to lose its shape, and then placed in a brazier, or vessel suitable for cooking over embers (see BRASA), with pieces of lard or ham, remnants of meats, carrots, onions and a small mixed bunch; it is moistened with concentrated broth (page 131), and left to boil for three hours over two fires; then it is drained, untied, covered with gelatin and served over tomato sauce à la française, or Spanish (see pages 765 and 778), or over cucumbers, endive or spinach, (see).
beef à la crème (Square of).
Once the piece is cut and the bones, skins and nerves that are on the tenderloin are removed, it is soaked in milk for twenty-four hours; at the moment of skewering it, it is taken out of the milk, dried, sprinkled with fine salt that has been mixed with a little grated nutmeg, and skewered on a thick rod or skewer that is laid on the spit.

WHITE PURSLANE. After the purslane’s leaves have been removed and separated well from their stems, they are put to boil with earth salt, and when they are well cooked, which will be known when they break down when rubbed with the fingers, they are set aside; a pot with butter is put on the fire, raw tomato and garlic are chopped very fine, and some heads of onion are cut into quarters; all this is put to fry in the butter, and when it is very fried, so that the inner skins of the tomato have curled up, the purslane is taken out of the pot and washed well in cold water;
*
they are drained, squeezed well and put to fry with the tomato; when they are well fried, pork broth is added to them, seasoned with fine salt, They are made just like lettuce in butter, and when it is, pork broth is added to it; a small piece of bread is fried in butter and ground with cloves, pepper and cumin, all of which is put in the pot and seasoned with fine salt; then the cooked pork meat is added and the purslane is left to season.
